1.q: בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁ⁠י אֶת־יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠כָל־קְ֝רָבַ֗⁠י אֶת־שֵׁ֥ם קָדְשֽׁ⁠וֹ
1.note: The phrases **Bless Yahweh, my soul** and **all of my inward parts, the name of his holiness** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Bless Yahweh, my soul! Yes, all of my inward parts, bless the name of his holiness]

David is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself] or [my inner being]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [bless the name of his holiness]
David is using the term **name** to refer to Yahweh’s holy person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his holy person]

Here, **all of my inward parts** represents David’s entire being from an internal perspective. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and everything that I am]

2.note: Here, **my soul** represents David’s entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself] or [my inner being]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could avoid using the double negative **do not forget** by expressing the idea in a positive form. Alternate translation: [and remember]

3.note: The pronoun **your** in verses 3–5 refers to “my soul” in verse 2. In this way, David is referring to himself. If “your” communicates the meaning well in your language, consider using that. Otherwise, consider using “my” here. Use the same translation decision for these phrases through verse 5. Alternate translation: [My soul, he is the one pardoning all your sins] or [He is the one pardoning all my sins]

4.note: Here, **life** represents the entire person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you]
Here, **the pit** represents death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from dying]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **mercy**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the one keeping his covenant to love you and be merciful to you]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a king placing a **crown** on the psalmist. He means that God is honoring and blessing him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one blessing you with] or [the one honoring you with]

5.note: The phrase **your ornaments** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. It seems that the scribe mistook the word translated as **ornaments** for a similar word that means “existence.” The ancient Greek translation says, “your desires.” You may want to follow one of those readings. Alternate translation: [your existence] or [your desires]

David is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean good things. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [with good things]

The word **itself** indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same thing fills two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [becomes renewed]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the eagle** is capable and strong, so **your youth** being renewed makes you feel capable and strong. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like an eagle that can go wherever it desires to go]

6.note: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, he is the one doing righteousness]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is right and just]

The expression **those being oppressed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people whom others are oppressing]

7.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he made known his deeds]

8.note: The psalmist is using **long of nostrils** as a common expression of his culture to mean “patient” or “slow to become angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [very patient]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and always faithful to his covenant with us]

9.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **contend** means to contend with us, his people. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He will not contend with us]

The implication is that God will not **contend** or remain angry for an unlimited length of time, but will eventually cease his anger. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the end of time]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will not maintain his anger]

10.q: לֹ֣א כַ֭⁠חֲטָאֵי⁠נוּ עָ֣שָׂה לָ֑⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א כַ֝⁠עֲוֺנֹתֵ֗י⁠נוּ גָּמַ֥ל עָלֵֽי⁠נוּ
10.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way, as in the UST. Otherwise, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [He does not deal with us according to our sins; let me say again, he does not treat us according to our iniquities]

10.q: לֹ֣א כַ֭⁠חֲטָאֵי⁠נוּ עָ֣שָׂה לָ֑⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א כַ֝⁠עֲוֺנֹתֵ֗י⁠נוּ גָּמַ֥ל עָלֵֽי⁠נוּ
10.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that people’s sins and iniquities deserve punishment from God. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He does not give punishment to us that is as bad as our sins, and he does not treat us as badly as our iniquities deserve]

11.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation of how great Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness is toward those who fear him. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [You see,]

11.q: כִּ֤י כִ⁠גְבֹ֣הַּ שָׁ֭מַיִם עַל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ גָּבַ֥ר חַ֝סְדּ֗⁠וֹ עַל־יְרֵאָֽי⁠ו
11.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the heavens** are extremely **high above the earth**, so **his covenant faithfulness** is extremely **strong toward those fearing him**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [For just as it is impossible to measure how high the heavens are above the earth, it is also impossible to measure how strong his covenant faithfulness is toward those fearing him]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that is how strongly committed he is to being faithful]

12.q: כִּ⁠רְחֹ֣ק מִ֭זְרָח מִֽ⁠מַּֽעֲרָ֑ב הִֽרְחִ֥יק מִ֝מֶּ֗⁠נּוּ אֶת־פְּשָׁעֵֽי⁠נוּ
12.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the sunrise** **from the sunset** is an immeasurable distance, so how far **he has removed our transgressions from us** is an immeasurable distance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as it is impossible to measure how far the sunrise is from the sunset, it is also impossible to measure how far he has removed our transgressions from us]

12.q: כִּ⁠רְחֹ֣ק מִ֭זְרָח מִֽ⁠מַּֽעֲרָ֑ב הִֽרְחִ֥יק מִ֝מֶּ֗⁠נּוּ אֶת־פְּשָׁעֵֽי⁠נוּ
12.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the sentence if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [As far as the sunrise is from the sunset, that is how far he has removed our transgressions from us]

13.q: כְּ⁠רַחֵ֣ם אָ֭ב עַל־בָּנִ֑ים רִחַ֥ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה עַל־יְרֵאָֽי⁠ו
13.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [As a father has compassion on his children, in the same way, Yahweh has compassion on those fearing him]

13.q: כְּ⁠רַחֵ֣ם אָ֭ב עַל־בָּנִ֑ים רִחַ֥ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה עַל־יְרֵאָֽי⁠ו
13.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a father has compassion on his children** very much, so also **Yahweh has compassion on those fearing him** very much. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As a father has constant and strong compassion on his children, so Yahweh has constant and strong compassion on those fearing him]

13.q: כְּ⁠רַחֵ֣ם אָ֭ב עַל־בָּנִ֑ים רִחַ֥ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה עַל
13.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [As a father loves his children, Yahweh loves]

14.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [You see,]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **form** refers to the physical nature and constitution of human beings. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the weakness of our form] or [what weak stuff we are made of]

The pronoun **he** in the phrase **he, he knows** refers to Yahweh. The repetition of the pronoun emphasizes that Yahweh, more than anyone else, knows the frailty of human beings. If your language has a way to express this emphasis naturally, you may want to use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [he, more than anyone, knows]

15.note: David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Any person]

Here, **days** represents a person’s lifetime. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his lifetime is like the lifetime of grass]

The psalmist is making a comparison to teach that just as **grass** lives for only a short time, so people live for only a short time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [his days are few, like the length of time that grass lives]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a flower of the field** flourishes for only a short time, so does a person’s life last for only a short time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a flower of the field, the time when he flourishes is short]

16.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation of how people are like grass and flowers. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]
The pronoun **it** refers to the flower. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the flower]

The psalmist is speaking of **its place** as if it were a person who could **acknowledge** something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and there is nothing in its place to indicate that it had been there]

17.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh will be faithful to his covenant from everlasting]

The psalmist is using **from everlasting to everlasting** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lasts forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he will be righteous]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the children of children** refers to future generations. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to their descendants]

18.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [to the ones keeping his covenant, that is, to the ones remembering his precepts, to do them]

The pronoun **the ones** refers to people who fear Yahweh, as described in verse 17. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to those children … and to the children] or [to those descendants … and to the descendants]

The implication is that they are actively keeping God’s precepts in their minds so that they can obey them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [keeping in mind]

Here, **to do them** marks this clause as the goal or purpose of **remembering his precepts**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to do them]

19.note: Here, **throne** represents the authority and power to rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is the supreme ruler]

Here, **kingdom** represents Yahweh ruling as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he, as king,]

20.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **listening to the voice of his word** means obeying what God says. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [obeying]

Here, **the voice of his word** represents what God says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he says]

21.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pleasure**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what pleases him]

22.note: The psalmist is speaking to **all his works** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about praising Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about all of Yahweh’s works. Alternate translation: [I want all of Yahweh’s works to bless him,]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **his reign**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the places where he reigns]

The psalmist is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my inner being]
